title: Within two links of a proven or charged case, and still paid
question: Which organizations and firms sit within two links of someone named in a proven or charged case and are still being paid by the City?
finding: 60 organizations and firms that the City paid in fiscal 2026 or 2027 are within two links of a person or organization named in the file of one of the 30 proven or charged cases. 3 are parties to a case in the record of case outcomes; 7 are named in a case file without being a party; 50 are not in any of those files and sit one or two links away. Together they were paid $1.19 billion in fiscal years that began after the case became public; $95.9 million of that went to parties.
how: Starting from every organization, firm or person a proven or charged case file names, the graph was walked one and two links out (hubs already removed). An organization or firm is listed if the City's ledger shows a payment to it in fiscal 2026 or 2027. The column “standing of the case” is the level of the case file, not of the organization. The next column says what the organization itself is: a party to the case only if the record of case outcomes (court, District Attorney, City Attorney and Ethics Commission documents) lists it as a party that was convicted, pleaded, admitted, stipulated or is charged; otherwise named in the file only; otherwise not in the file at all. The date a case became public is the first enforcement event in the case file's timeline; the amount paid afterwards adds only the fiscal years that began after that date, so it is a floor. Where two cases reach the same organization the shorter path is shown. Built on the graph described under “The linked groups”: organizations, firms, San Francisco addresses and people (officers, registered lobbyists and consultants, officials) joined by eleven kinds of recorded link, each with its source. Public bodies, banks, utilities, insurers, law and accounting firms, universities, hospitals, office buildings, and any node tied to more than 12 others by one kind of link were removed first. A person appears only on a rare full name, in a public role on file, with a second independent record for each tie, and is always a name match. A member is called a party only if the record of case outcomes lists it as one; being named in a case file is shown separately. Groups are the connected sets that remain, or the tightly linked cores of sets larger than 40.
limits: Being linked is not being involved: nonprofits share board members, buildings and auditors all the time, and San Francisco is a small city. A group is a place to look, ranked by how many independent signs sit inside it. Being named in the file of a charged or proven case is not being charged: the people charged are individuals, and the organizations in their files include fiscal sponsors, grantees and employers that were never accused. Being near a case is not being part of it: most rows are tied to someone in a file by an address, a donation, a requested payment or a shared board name. One organization settled and stayed eligible, and the proceeding against another was dismissed. A charge is an allegation. Where one case file gathers several cases, the date used is the earliest of them, which can be earlier than the event that concerns a given organization. Drawn together in a case file: a case file also names bystanders, victims and people who were cleared. Same street address: nonprofit centres, landlords and tenants, and fiscal sponsors share buildings. Payment at an official's request: officials must disclose charitable payments they ask for. Gives to the campaign of: campaign donations are reported, with limits on amounts. Pays (grant, contract or rent): sub-grants and specialist contractors are how programmes are delivered.
